distractors: The highest-priority items on a plan of work, the ones that get finished before anything else is started.
Costs a change imposes on people who were never party to it and are not compensated for it, which is why they rarely show up in anyone's numbers.
Results large enough to be worth measuring at all, as against the ones that vanish into the noise. It is a threshold about size, and where you set it decides what gets reported and what does not.

The order in which dependent changes have to be made, so that nothing is switched on before the thing it relies on exists. It is a sequencing constraint, and getting it wrong is how a rollout stalls halfway through a weekend.

The group who receive a change before anyone else and whose experience decides whether it goes further: a floor, a region, a single desk. Who goes first is chosen deliberately, usually for tolerance rather than for how representative they are.
The phase of a rollout that comes after the pilot, when a change finally goes to everyone who was not in the trial.
Risks a team identifies in advance, writes down, and asks a sponsor to accept formally, so that if one of them lands nobody can claim they were not told.

The extra cost of running something at a larger size: more storage, more support, more licences, all of it arriving in proportion to the growth. It is arithmetic rather than surprise, and a competent team can forecast it a year out.

Outcomes that were foreseen and then judged too small to act on, which is a decision somebody actually made rather than something the analysis missed. They tend to resurface in a review a year later, where the argument is about whether the judgement was reasonable at the time.

A follow-on tranche of funding released only once the first has proved out, so that money arrives in stages tied to evidence rather than all at once on the strength of a plan. It is a control a board puts on a programme it believes in but does not yet trust, and it is negotiated at the outset.
